ai-at-work.title: Claude Code costs up to $200 a month. Goose does the same thing for free.
ai-at-work.excerpt: The artificial intelligence coding revolution comes with a catch: it's expensive.Claude Code, Anthropic's terminal-based AI agent that can write, debug, and deploy code autonomously, has captured the
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic's Claude Code is charging developers up to $200 monthly for AI-assisted coding while competitors like Goose offer identical functionality for free. This matters because your developers will absolutely notice when they can get the same work done without dropping serious cash, and you'll have to justify Claude's premium if you're considering it for your teams. Here's the thing: pricing doesn't win wars in the developer tools space, features do, but when features are basically equal, price becomes the only argument you've got left.

ai-at-work.title: Salesforce rolls out new Slackbot AI agent as it battles Microsoft and Google in workplace AI
ai-at-work.excerpt: Salesforce on Tuesday launched an entirely rebuilt version of Slackbot, the company's workplace assistant, transforming it from a simple notification tool into what executives describe as a fully powe
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Salesforce rebuilt Slackbot from a basic notification tool into an AI agent that can search data, draft documents, and take actions within Slack for Business+ and Enterprise+ customers. This matters because workplace AI assistants are becoming table stakes, and every major vendor is racing to embed intelligent automation into the tools where people actually work. Here's the thing though: we've heard this "AI agent" story before, and most employees still just want their Slack notifications to work properly without drowning in bot clutter.

ai-at-work.title: Anthropic launches Cowork, a Claude Desktop agent that works in your files — no coding required
ai-at-work.excerpt: Anthropic released Cowork on Monday, a new AI agent capability that extends the power of its wildly successful Claude Code tool to non-technical users — and according to company insiders, the team bui
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic released Cowork, an AI agent that lets non-technical users automate file-based tasks in Claude Desktop without writing code. This matters because digital workplace leaders are drowning in requests to integrate AI into daily workflows, and a no-code agent tool actually addresses real user pain instead of adding another chatbot to the pile. The fact they built it in ten days using their own AI tools is either impressive or terrifying depending on how you feel about AI eating its own lunch.

ai-at-work.title: The creator of Claude Code just revealed his workflow, and developers are losing their minds
ai-at-work.excerpt: When the creator of the world's most advanced coding agent speaks, Silicon Valley doesn't just listen — it takes notes.For the past week, the engineering community has been dissecting a thread on X fr
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Boris Cherny from Anthropic shared his personal coding workflow on X and developers went nuts dissecting it like it was the Rosetta Stone of productivity. This matters because digital workplace leaders are always hunting for ways to boost developer efficiency, and when influential figures publicize their methods, it shapes what tools and practices get adopted across teams. Here's the thing though: someone's personal workflow is basically their personal preference, and I've seen plenty of cargo cult adopters waste time copying setups that don't fit their actual problems or team dynamics.

tools-tech.title: Microsoft business software faces UK antitrust probe over bundling, AI lock-in
tools-tech.excerpt: The UK’s competition regulator has launched a broad antitrust investigation into Microsoft’s business software ecosystem, opening a new front in growing regulatory scrutiny of how cloud platforms, pro
tools-tech.dwp_take: The UK's Competition and Markets Authority has launched an antitrust investigation into Microsoft's bundling practices around cloud, productivity software, and AI capabilities. This matters because it directly impacts enterprise software licensing strategies and could reshape how organizations access and pay for Microsoft tools going forward. Look, Microsoft's been playing the bundling game for decades, but now they've got AI sprinkled on top and regulators are finally asking uncomfortable questions about whether that's competition or just lock-in with better marketing.

tools-tech.title: The trouble with emotion-reading AI
tools-tech.excerpt: “If you can’t measure it, you can’t fix it.” That’s a common saying in business, and it tends to be true. But what if the thing you want to fix is your employees’ attitudes? The AI revolution makes it
tools-tech.dwp_take: A bunch of vendors are pitching emotion-reading AI as a way to measure and improve employee attitudes and mental states. This matters because if you're considering deploying this stuff in your organization, you need to know that these systems are notoriously unreliable and create legitimate privacy concerns that will tank morale faster than they'll ever improve it. Here's the thing: if your employee engagement is so broken that you need a machine to guess how people feel instead of, you know, actually talking to them, you've already got much bigger problems than AI can solve.

tools-tech.title: Windows 11 Insider Previews: What’s in the latest build?
tools-tech.excerpt: Windows 11 25H2 has been publicly released, but behind the scenes, Microsoft is constantly working to improve the newest version of Windows. The company frequently rolls out preview builds to members
tools-tech.dwp_take: Microsoft's releasing Windows 11 25H2 while simultaneously pushing preview builds through the Insider Program to test what comes next. Digital workplace teams need to pay attention because these previews signal what management will eventually expect them to deploy, and getting ahead of the curve means fewer fires to fight later. The real question is whether your organization has the appetite to actually test these builds or if you'll just wait until Microsoft makes it mandatory and then scramble like you always do.

tools-tech.title: Apple’s App Store model for AI
tools-tech.excerpt: Apple has a design for AI life. It hopes to build on the outstanding hardware performance its systems already provide to create a fantastic environment in which AI developers can thrive. If this plan
tools-tech.dwp_take: Apple is positioning itself as the gatekeeper for AI applications through a curated marketplace model similar to its App Store, controlling which AI tools can run on its devices. This matters to digital workplace pros because it will shape which AI capabilities your workforce can actually access on Apple devices, and it gives one company significant power over what enterprise AI solutions are even available to you. Look, we've seen this movie before with the App Store, and spoiler alert: walled gardens are great for the company building the walls and considerably less great for everyone trying to actually get work done on the other side of them.

digital-culture.title: ‘Too busy’ all of the time? Here’s how to get things done and make space for fun
digital-culture.excerpt: Below, Laura Vanderkam shares five key insights from her new book, Big Time: A Simple Path to Time Abundance. Laura is the author of several time management books and the host of the Before Breakfast
digital-culture.dwp_take: Laura Vanderkam's latest book argues that feeling perpetually swamped is often a planning problem, not a time problem, and offers frameworks for better time management and creating space for things beyond work. This matters to digital workplace leaders because burned-out employees driving constant connectivity actually tank productivity and engagement, so helping teams work smarter rather than just harder becomes a talent retention issue. Here's the thing though: most organizations that preach work-life balance still measure success by how quickly you respond to Slack at 9 p.m., so until that culture shifts, no time management book will actually fix the real problem.

digital-culture.title: Do you ever think about the paths you didn’t take?
digital-culture.excerpt: A few weeks ago, I was reconnecting with a former colleague from my higher education days, and we started talking about our current work. At one point, she paused and said, “I love the path you’ve tak
digital-culture.dwp_take: This piece explores how career paths shift unexpectedly over time, using a personal reflection on what-could-have-beens in professional life. For digital workplace folks, it's a reminder that the skills and experiences you build today might fuel completely different roles tomorrow, so don't get too precious about job titles. Here's the thing though: spend less time wondering about the dean position you didn't take and more time building the kind of workplace where people actually want to work, because that's the career move that actually matters.

digital-culture.title: Managers are unprepared to lead a human-agent hybrid workforce
digital-culture.excerpt: Andrew Reece, Chief AI Scientist, BetterUp The introduction of AI agents into the corporate workforce is not like other technology disruptions. Unlike previous automation, agents are empowered to act
digital-culture.dwp_take: A new study found that most managers lack the skills and frameworks needed to effectively supervise teams that include AI agents working alongside humans. This matters because as AI agents take on autonomous decision-making roles, managers need entirely different approaches to oversight, accountability, and team dynamics than what worked with traditional automation. Here's the thing though: we've been saying "managers need new skills" for fifteen years with every technology wave, and most organizations still haven't figured out basic email management, so expecting widespread readiness on AI agents feels optimistic at best.

digital-culture.title: The hidden cost of workplace transformation: How change initiatives crush top employees
digital-culture.excerpt: Nearly half of employees report experiencing "transformation fatigue," according to a recent study
digital-culture.dwp_take: So half your workforce is burned out from constant change initiatives and nobody's surprised anymore. This matters because those top performers you're trying to impress with your shiny new digital workplace tools are actually the ones most likely to quit when transformation fatigue sets in, which defeats the whole purpose. Here's the thing: transformation doesn't need to be a five-ring circus with new platforms launching every quarter. Sometimes the best digital workplace strategy is knowing when to stop changing things and let people actually work.

industry-news.title: This week in 5 numbers: Half of job applicants want to ban or heavily regulate ATS
industry-news.excerpt: Here’s a roundup of numbers from the last week of HR news — including how many managers said they never received training on how to ask for feedback.
industry-news.dwp_take: Half of job applicants now want to ban or heavily regulate applicant tracking systems, according to recent HR data. This matters because your ATS is literally the first impression candidates have of your organization, and if they're already frustrated before they even apply, you're losing talent before round one. Here's the thing: most ATS systems were designed by people who clearly never actually used them, and candidates know it.

industry-news.title: Employers say they’re doing enough to help with medical costs, but workers disagree
industry-news.excerpt: Companies could see lower productivity, increased absenteeism and higher turnover as employees face financial stress, Prudential Financial said.
industry-news.dwp_take: Companies are telling themselves they're handling employee healthcare costs just fine while workers are clearly struggling financially and losing sleep over it. This gap matters because when your workforce is stressed about medical bills, they're not focused on their jobs, they're calling out sick more often, and your replacement costs are climbing. The real issue isn't what employers think they're doing, it's what employees actually experience, and right now there's a canyon between those two things.

industry-news.title: Reports of misconduct have spiked — and cases are getting more complex, study finds
industry-news.excerpt: To create lasting change, employee relations teams must effectively handle a greater volume of investigations and reach workers who don’t speak up, HR Acuity’s CEO said.
industry-news.dwp_take: Misconduct reports are up and investigations are getting messier, according to HR Acuity's latest research. This matters to digital workplace folks because you're now the folks building the systems that document, track, and manage these cases, which means compliance, security, and privacy just got a whole lot more complicated on your platform. Here's the thing: better reporting tools are great, but if your culture still discourages people from speaking up in the first place, you're just building a faster way to document the same broken trust.

industry-news.title: Employers adopt AI tools faster than they can train workers to use them
industry-news.excerpt: This “productivity paradox” is one reason artificial intelligence ROI remains somewhat elusive, Randstad Digital said in its report.
industry-news.dwp_take: Companies are rolling out AI tools without giving employees the training they need to actually use them effectively. This matters because you're about to spend a lot of money on software licenses while your workforce fumbles around trying to figure out what the tools even do. It's like handing someone a Ferrari and expecting them to win a race without ever teaching them to drive, which explains why your AI investment probably won't deliver the returns you promised the CFO.
